Don't re-resolve `object` on every non-generic serialize (2.3 KB/call, ~40x) (#1280)

RuntimeTypeModel caches serializer lookups, but only POSITIVE ones: the cache is a
Hashtable, so a miss and a cached null are indistinguishable, and GetServicesSlow
stores a result only `if (service is not null)`. A type with no service therefore
re-runs the entire slow path - a lock, the repeated-provider probe, and
FindOrAddAuto - every single time it is asked for.

typeof(object) is exactly such a type, and the non-generic API asks for it on every
call: the typed lookup misses, and only then does the dynamic path resolve the
concrete type. So `Serialize<object>` / the object-typed overloads cost ~2.9us and
allocate 2272 bytes per call, against ~72ns and zero for the same serialization
reached generically. For a service pushing 10k messages/sec through the non-generic
API that is ~22 MB/s of GC pressure for no work.

Fixed by returning early for typeof(object), which is the one type where "has no
service" is guaranteed rather than merely true today: Add(typeof(object)) is refused
outright ("You cannot reconfigure System.Object"), so it can never acquire one. A
new test pins that restriction, because if it were ever lifted the shortcut would
silently start answering wrongly and nothing else would notice.

Deliberately NOT generalised to "cache every negative lookup". That is the bigger
win - it would also help the auxiliary-type paths - but a type that is unknown now
may be added later, and ResetServiceCache is only invoked from a couple of MetaType
paths, so memoising misses in general needs invalidation that does not currently
exist. Worth doing separately, with tests for that.

Measured before and after with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread: 2272.0 B/call
-> 0.0 B/call, for both a Stream and an IBufferWriter destination. The allocation
assertion in the new test is the regression guard and was verified to fail without
the fix (2296 B/call); it is guarded to net5.0+ since that API is, while the
semantic tests run on every TFM.

* Codegen respects editions: every decision point now asks ResolvedFeatures

Goal 3 of the editions work. Feature resolution is extracted to
FileDescriptorProto.ResolveFeatures() - idempotent, driven purely by
descriptor data - so it also runs at Generate() time for sets loaded
from compiled descriptors that never went through Process(). The
legacy inference grows proto3-optional => explicit presence, making
ResolvedFeatures the single answer for every syntax.

The five decision points that used to branch on the syntax string:

- presence tracking (TrackFieldPresence): explicit presence, however
  spelled - proto2, proto3-optional, or the editions default;
- packedness: new IsPackedField() over resolved features (the
  syntax-based overload remains for the shipped public API);
- delimited: message-typed fields with message_encoding=DELIMITED get
  DataFormat.Group - the headline match, since editions delimited
  fields arrive as TYPE_MESSAGE, not TYPE_GROUP;
- required: IsRequired from field_presence=LEGACY_REQUIRED;
- enum defaults: keyed on the *enum's* closed-ness rather than the
  field's file syntax (also more correct across files).

C# and VB both, pinned by EditionsCodeGenTests: explicit/implicit/
required presence shapes, packed/expanded, delimited, and closed-enum
first-value defaults all verified in the generated code.

* The schema-writer speaks editions (goal 4, the stretch)

GetSchema/GetProto accept ProtoSyntax.Edition2023/Edition2024; the
emitted dialect:

- `edition = "2023"` header (2024 additionally opts out of STYLE2024
  naming enforcement, since the names come from .NET members);
- bare fields (explicit presence is the editions default); IsRequired
  becomes [features.field_presence = LEGACY_REQUIRED];
- DataFormat.Group / SupportNull / NullWrappedValueGroup members emit
  [features.message_encoding = DELIMITED] instead of the 'group'

* Build-time gRPC proxies and server bindings, hung off a declared partial

Reworks the approach in protobuf-net#1255 / protobuf-net.Grpc#364 (Victor
Irzak, @virzak) around a consumer-declared type rather than a process-wide
registry. The contract parse, shape classification and per-operation emit
bodies are adapted from that work and credited in the files that borrow them.

Why the reshape: a registry leaves the payload marshallers resolving through
MarshallerCache.CreateMarshaller<T> -> CanSerialize(typeof(T)) ->
DynamicStub -> MakeGenericType, whose failure is swallowed into "no, can't
serialize that". Under native AOT that is not a fallback, it is
"No marshaller available for X" at startup - demonstrated by publishing
src/AotGrpcSmoke natively before the pre-population below was added.

The shape mirrors [ProtoModel]: the consumer declares

    [ProtoGrpc(Model = typeof(MyModel))]
    [ProtoService(typeof(IGreeter), typeof(GreeterService))]
    public sealed partial class MyServices : ClientFactory { }

and gets client proxies, an IServiceMethodProvider<TImpl> per implementation,
and an AddMyServices() registration extension. Nothing resolves by Type at run
time: no registry, no [ModuleInitializer], and no MakeGenericMethod on the
server path (naming the implementation closes those generics statically).

This needs *no* changes to protobuf-net.Grpc. ClientFactory is already an
abstract class with the two members we override, and Grpc.AspNetCore.Server
registers IServiceMethodProvider<T> through TryAddEnumerable, so a generated
provider is simply added alongside. The trigger attributes are generator-owned
for now (post-init, internal per assembly), which is the path [ProtoModel]
took; an internal copy wins name resolution over a public one in a referenced
assembly, so moving them later is not a break.

Marshallers are pre-registered onto the BinderConfiguration via the public
SetMarshaller<T>, sidestepping the Type-keyed probe entirely - this is
load-bearing, not an optimisation.

* Record the two-direction seeding design, and why [ProtoSerializable] must not evaporate

Design only; nothing behavioural here beyond a doc comment.

The principle is the useful part and is worth keeping wider than the payload set:
if a consumer says "use this model", we should check that we think it is going to
work. Naming a model is a claim about another file - possibly another assembly -
and every part of it is checkable at compile time.

Two directions:

* model in this compilation - infer the seeds, and warn if it is not marked
  [ProtoModel] at all (today that fails as a bare CS0117 on the generated
  Instance);
* model in a referenced assembly - nothing can be added to it, so check it and
  warn per payload type it cannot serialize.

Checked rather than assumed, and it changes the design: for the second direction
the thing to read is the emitted ISerializer<T> set, not [ProtoSerializable].
A generated model carries a nested `private sealed class ProtoBufGeneratedServices
: ISerializer<T1>, ...`, and Roslyn sees private nested types through metadata.
That is what the model can actually do; the attribute is only what it was asked to
do, and the two differ both ways - a dropped seed (PBN3001) keeps its attribute,
and a payload reached transitively as a member of another seed never had one, so
an attribute check false-positives on a model that is completely fine.

On the [Conditional] question: neither ProtoModelAttribute nor
ProtoSerializableAttribute is, so both reach metadata today. Agreed that this
feature justifies keeping it that way, so the reason is now recorded on the
attribute itself - adding [Conditional] later would be invisible here and would
silently delete the cross-assembly check.

Also noted while checking: no fixture has a void or no-arg operation, so the one
place ProtoBuf.Grpc.Internal.Empty appears is unmeasured. The handling is right -

* Drop the [Conditional] claim from ProtoSerializableAttribute; the design does not rely on it

* Investigate the interceptor attribute encoding: the Roslyn baseline does not have to move

The doubt was that the new [InterceptsLocation(version, data)] form has a Roslyn helper
behind it, where the old (path, line, char) form was directly synthesizable - forcing a
newer Roslyn reference, which is what lets BuildTools.Legacy serve old SDKs.

The v1 data encoding is fully specified and has now been reproduced exactly, verified by
building both ours and the real API's output and comparing strings. That pinned the two
details the spec leaves implicit, and I had both wrong at first:

* the checksum is xxHash128 of the text as UTF-16 code units, not UTF-8 - "content
  checksum of the file" reads like bytes-on-disk and is not;
* the position is the *name node's* Position (FullSpan.Start), not the invocation's: for
  "x".Trim() it is Trim's position, where the invocation's is several characters earlier;
* the display name is Path.GetFileName(tree.FilePath), checked across an absolute, a
  nested and a relative path.

Only the checksum and position have to be right - the compiler matches on those and uses
the display name for diagnostics only - and a wrong value is a compile error in the
consumer's build rather than a silent miss.

xxHash128 is the only piece 4.3.1 lacks, and Roslyn vendors its own copy
(Compilers/Core/Portable/Hashing/XxHash128.cs plus XxHashShared.cs and
XxHash64.State.cs, MIT, already building for netstandard-targeting assemblies). Lifting
those three avoids a System.IO.Hashing package reference, which for an analyzer means
shipping a dll alongside - the pain that made BuildTools compile Core's sources in.

But reflection is probably sufficient and is the better answer, and the version numbers
are the reason: the (version, data) form and GetInterceptableLocation arrived together in
4.11, so any host that would accept what we emit already has the API. The analyzer binds
to the host's Roslyn at run time - the same reason ProtoModelGenerator spells
LanguageVersion.CSharp12 numerically - so it can call the API reflectively when present
and synthesize otherwise. That also avoids betting on v1 staying readable, which
synthesis alone would.

Out-of-band sub-types for the AOT generator: [ProtoSubType] (#1317)

* Out-of-band sub-types for the AOT generator: [ProtoSubType]

protobuf-net#1308. [ProtoInclude] goes on the base type, so it can only describe a
hierarchy whose base is able to name its sub-types. It cannot when the sub-type lives
in a package the base library does not reference, or is a generic construction like
Tagged<Order> that no base library could have written down. At runtime that is what
AddSubType is for; the compile-time model had no equivalent, which is where the ticket
came in.

[ProtoSubType(typeof(Base), typeof(Sub), fieldNumber)] is that equivalent, and the
outcome is exactly as though the base had carried [ProtoInclude(fieldNumber,
typeof(Sub))] all along. It is generator-only: the runtime model does not honour it,
exactly as it does not honour [ProtoSurrogate].

The merge is done in TryGetSubTypes, and that is the whole trick. It is the single
choke point GetLinkedBases and GetHierarchyRoot run through, so by the time anything
downstream sees a link it cannot tell where the link came from - the emitter needed no
change at all, and the is-chain, the sub-type switch and the group framing all fall out
unchanged. That also makes seeding unnecessary, which the design note had assumed would
be mandatory: reaching the base enqueues the sub-types as reachable, and seeding a
sub-type finds the base through GetLinkedBases, so either end is enough.
ProtoSubTypeReferenceTests pins both directions, and the Data/ fixture seeds neither.

The sites are [ProtoSurrogate]'s, plus module: referenced assemblies (and their
modules), this assembly, its module, then the model. Scanning assembly and module
attributes is cheap and bounded, where scanning every type in every reference would not
be. Where the surrogate precedent misleads is the merge - surrogates override, includes
accumulate - so two packages each adding a sub-type to one base give a hierarchy with
both. An exact restatement of an existing declaration is absorbed rather than reported,
since a consumer repeating what a reference already offers is a fair thing to write.

It is deliberately not the generic [ProtoInclude<A, B>(100)] spelling the ticket
proposed, and the reason is worth recording: generic attributes compile fine on every
one of Core's TFMs, but on .NET Framework GetCustomAttributes on *any* member carrying
a generic attribute throws NotSupportedException: Generic types are not valid - not for
the generic one alone, for the whole call. AttributeMap.Create is GetCustomAttributes,
on types and on assemblies, so a generic spelling reachable from a contract type would
take out a net4x consumer's runtime model with an exception naming nothing relevant.
An attribute with no runtime meaning must not be able to do that. Probed with a net462
console app rather than reasoned about; CustomAttributeData is unaffected, and so is
net8.0.

The framing argument is a bool rather than a DataFormat, since a sub-type is always a
sub-message: length-prefixed versus delimited is the only choice there is, and the
other DataFormat values would silently mean nothing. "Left to protobuf-net" is told
from "explicitly length-prefixed" by constructor arity, which is why it is an overload
rather than an optional argument; nothing consumes that distinction yet, but it is in
the metadata if the default framing ever moves.

Validation is MetaType.AddSubType's, in its order, and every refusal matches
protobuf-net rather than falling short of it: a field number outside 1-536870911, a
sealed or non-class base ("Sub-types can only be added to non-sealed classes"), and a
sub-type that does not derive from the base ("is not a valid sub-type of") - which also
catches a type declared as a sub-type of itself. A bad declaration is recorded against
the base and reported only if that base is actually reached, because a declaration
lives on an assembly and reporting eagerly would warn about a library's mistake in
every model that references it. It reports PBN3002 and drops the base, which cascades
to the sub-types: a half-linked hierarchy is worse than none, since an unlinked
sub-type emits standalone and silently disagrees on the wire. Reservations and the
surrogate-with-inheritance refusal come along for free, being downstream of the merge.

Duplicate detection now covers both surfaces at once, which is new for [ProtoInclude]
too: two sub-types at one field number, or one sub-type named twice, previously reached
the emitter and produced a duplicate switch label. It runs after the DerivesFrom
filtering, which matters - a generic base's includes are shared by every closed
construction and only one of them applies to each. PBN0003/PBN0011 are errors, so no
compiling source tree can contain one, and the corpus did not move.

PBN0013 had to be taught about this. "The base-type is a proto-contract, but no include
is declared for X" fired on every sub-type linked this way, nagging people to write the
one attribute they cannot write; an assembly-level or module-level declaration now
satisfies it. A declaration on a model class does not, and that is a real limit rather
than an oversight - DataContractAnalyzer reports this from a syntax-node action, which
has no cheap way to find every [ProtoModel] in a compilation. The fixture carries a
#pragma and says so. Note the diagnostic already fired for anyone using runtime
AddSubType, so this narrows a pre-existing false positive rather than introducing one.

The replay is in all three harnesses - AotRefGen, AotConformanceTests and
AotDifferential - through the public MetaType.AddSubType, beside the surrogate replay.
Without it the reference model has never heard of the linkage and serializes the
sub-type as a standalone contract, which reads as a generator fault and is the
opposite. Only the first two have anything to replay today; the corpus one is there so
that the next thing added to it cannot be mis-diagnosed, which is a trap this harness
has already fallen into once.

Covered by a differential fixture (mixed surfaces on one base, a closed generic
sub-type, group framing, and nothing seeded but the holder), a diagnostics fixture per
refusal, the assembly and module spellings in isolation, and five cross-assembly tests
that need genuinely separate compilations. Corpus differential unchanged at 100% match.

* Document [ProtoSubType], and correct the design note it came from

docs/aot.md gets the user-facing half, under "things that catch people out" beside the
surrogate section it is a sibling of: the shape, the three sites, and the two ways it
differs from [ProtoSurrogate] - declarations accumulate rather than override, and your
model stops being determined by your own source, since adding a package reference can
change what a base-typed member puts on the wire. It also says outright that the
runtime model does not honour it, because someone using both models needs to keep
calling AddSubType.

notes/aot/findings.md had this as a "future idea" with the syntax left open, and two
parts of it were wrong once built rather than merely undecided, so the entry now says
what happened instead of what was planned. The open question - whether generic
attributes are safe given Core's TFMs - had a sharper answer than expected: they
compile everywhere, and it is *reflection* that breaks, on any member carrying one, for
the whole GetCustomAttributes call. And seeding, recorded there as mandatory, turned
out to be unnecessary: merging at the choke point makes a hierarchy self-seeding from
either end. The note was written before that merge point was worked out, which is worth
leaving visible - it is the second time here that a design note's "must" has turned out
to be an inference.

AGENTS.md gets the maintainer half, as a subsection of the inheritance notes, since
that is where anyone touching TryGetSubTypes will be looking.

* [ProtoSubType].IsGroup is three-state, so say so: bool?

The property collapsed "explicitly length-prefixed" and "not stated" into false, while the
metadata kept them apart by constructor arity - so the API was quietly less precise than
what it was recording. Both are length-prefixed today, which is exactly why the
distinction is worth keeping: if the default framing ever moves, an explicit false has to
stay explicit, and a bool would have made that a decision we had already taken by
accident.

null is the three-argument constructor, i.e. "left to protobuf-net". The generator is
unaffected either way - it reads the constructor arguments, not the property - and the
three ref-emit replays now test `is true` rather than unboxing, since null and false mean
the same thing to AddSubType today.

* PBN0013 knows about [ProtoSubType] at every site, and links to a rule page

The narrowing I put in first covered the assembly and module sites and left the
model-class one out, on the grounds that an analyzer reporting from a syntax-node action
has no cheap way to find every [ProtoModel] in a compilation. That was wrong twice over:
AnalysisContext does have RegisterCompilationStartAction - the comment in this very file
claiming otherwise is what I took it from - and AotMigrationAnalyzer has been walking
compilation.Assembly.GlobalNamespace from one since it shipped.

So the declarations are gathered compilation-wide now: assembly attributes, module
attributes, and every type the compilation declares, which is what reaches a declaration
on a model. It is built lazily and forced only by a PBN0013 candidate - a sub-type whose
base declares no include for it - so most compilations never walk anything, which is
strictly less work than the analyzer that set the precedent does unconditionally.

Matching is on each side's OriginalDefinition, because a declaration names a closed
construction (Tagged<int>) while this diagnostic is reported against the open declaration
it came from (Tagged<T>); a plain symbol comparison never matches, and the fixture kept
warning about exactly the shape the ticket is about. PBN0012 has a test for the same trap
on generic interfaces. Nothing is lost by the loosening - the open declaration is the only
place there is to report, so "some construction of this is declared" is the most that can
usefully be said.

The message now names the routes rather than only the flag, and carries a helpLinkUri to
docs/rules/PBN0013.md - a per-rule page, following the layout DapperAOT uses. The message
has to stay short, and the part that needs room is the case no analyzer can decide:
sub-types registered at another layer, through AddSubType on a RuntimeTypeModel, where
this warning is expected and should be ignored. The page also covers what the diagnostic
is actually protecting against, which is easy to lose sight of - an undeclared sub-type is
not a hard failure, it silently drops every inherited member.

The fixture's #pragma is gone, since there is nothing left to suppress.

The extension APIs read packed data (#1328) (#1329)

Extensible.GetValue/GetValues see one field at a time, so they read a repeated
scalar one value per field header - which rejects the packed encoding outright,
throwing "Invalid wire-type (String)". protoc has always written repeated
packable custom options packed, so this refused data every other implementation
treats as ordinary; it surfaced now because our own schema parser started
emitting packed enum options to match protoc, leaving it unable to read back the
descriptors it had just produced.

Both read paths learn the same inference the repeated serializers already make -
a length-delimited payload for a type whose own wire type is not length-delimited
is packed data:

- the typed path (TryGetExtendedValuesTyped) via a new State.TryReadPackedScalar,
  which is ReadPackedScalar reached without a list to read into;
- the reflective path, which generated accessors take whenever the field declares
  a DataFormat, via TypeModel.ReadAuxValues. That one drains the tag in a single
  pass, because TryDeserializeAuxiliaryType returns one value per call and would
  leave the reader parked mid-run.

Reading is widened, not changed: the expanded encoding, mixed encodings for one
tag, and string/bytes/message extensions all behave exactly as before, and
AppendValue still writes expanded. Declared packedness is deliberately not
consulted - the spec requires accepting either form regardless, which is why
PrepareToReadRepeated does not consult it either.

Verified against protoc 35.1 and Google.Protobuf as oracles: both pack repeated
packable options, including unary runs.

Two divergences measured while here and left alone, both write-side:
- the parser emits one packed run per value where protoc emits a single merged
  run, and packs only enums where protoc packs every packable scalar. Pinned in
  PackedCustomOptions so that closing it is a visible change.
- RepeatedSerializer writes a unary IsPacked list expanded, where protoc and
  Google.Protobuf pack it. Changing that would move bytes on the wire for
  existing contracts, so it stays.

FileDescriptorSet.Serialize(TypeModel, Stream, bool) has been public for
years, but nothing in this package could supply the TypeModel: we reference
protobuf-net.Core, which has no concrete model. So the only way to serialize
a descriptor set was to take a dependency on protobuf-net itself, purely to
reach RuntimeTypeModel.Default - for a type this package already has a
generated serializer for.

One static fixes that, and returns TypeModel rather than the generated class,
so CustomProtogenSerializer and its member surface stay internal. Everything
TypeModel offers comes with it: Deserialize over Stream, ReadOnlyMemory and
ReadOnlySequence, Serialize to IBufferWriter, DeepClone.

Deliberately not adding a Serialize(Stream, bool) overload. The parameter
order on the existing one is awkward - model first, so it cannot be given a
default - but it works, and a second spelling of the same call is not worth
the surface.

Tests confirm the round trip, that includeImports still filters through it
(the one thing a bare TypeModel cannot do, since it narrows Files rather than
changing how they are written), and that it produces byte-identical output to

* notes: initial Connect (connectrpc) investigation

Desk investigation only - nothing built or run. Follows the notes/aot layout:
a topic folder with a findings.md that opens with a Handover.

The findings that would change a decision:

- gRPC's HTTP/2 requirement comes from trailers alone, and Connect uses none;
  unary and single-direction streaming run on HTTP/1.1, only bidi needs HTTP/2.
- There is no .NET implementation, official or community.
- JSON is optional: connect-go clients default to binary, and the conformance
  suite takes features.codecs: [CODEC_PROTO] and skips the JSON matrix. So the
  long pole (protobuf-net has no JSON at all) is off the critical path.
- The generated gRPC proxies are protocol-blind - everything goes through
  Grpc.Core.CallInvoker - so a ConnectCallInvoker would give Connect to every
  existing protobuf-net.Grpc client with no generator or consumer changes.

Considered and dropped, recorded so they are not rediscovered as oversights:
build-time descriptor emission (nothing in Connect consumes a schema at run
time, and the build-time .proto is already reachable via RuntimeTypeModel), and
server reflection (optional, and already an open item against
protobuf-net.Grpc.Reflection).

Connect error details are google.protobuf.Any with the type-URL prefix
trimmed, which surfaces a real weakness: protobuf-net has no Any support, no
Package on [ProtoContract], and computes a type's qualified name per GetSchema
call from the requested type set - so it is not a stable wire identity today.

* notes/connect: live protocol probe, and a staged MVP path

Probed demo.connectrpc.com (connect-go, public, no toolchain) rather than
reasoning about the spec:

- binary unary over forced HTTP/1.1 returns 200 with Content-Length and no
  trailers - the claim the whole case rests on is now evidence;
- the request and response bodies are the bare message, no envelope. The
  request bytes 0a 02 68 69 are exactly what protobuf-net emits for the
  equivalent contract;
- a malformed body gives 400 + application/json + {"code":"invalid_argument"},
  but an unknown method gives 404 + text/plain with no error object at all -
  which is why the spec has an HTTP-status inference table, and means a client
  assuming every non-200 carries JSON will throw on the most ordinary failure.

connectconformance ships as a single statically-linked binary per platform, so
the external oracle is CI-gatable without a Go toolchain.

MVP path staged so each step is falsifiable externally before the next depends
on it, and no Roslyn work happens until the shape it must emit is known to
work: client against Eliza, then the hand-written target output reviewed and
frozen, then the generator, then conformance plus an AOT smoke test.

Decision: the first MVP covers unary only, but every method shape is expected
eventually, so stage 1 must not preclude them. Five traps recorded, each of
which works for unary and cannot be extended: a buffer-shaped transport with no
seam for framing; a Task<TResponse> Handle(TRequest) server signature that no
streaming shape can reach; assuming trailers are response headers (true for
unary, false for streaming, where they arrive in EndStreamResponse); assuming
Content-Length is knowable; and deciding errors at three separate throw sites
when unary, streaming and an unrouted 404 all present differently.

before the code exists.

* notes/connect: record why there are no marshallers

HandWritten.cs names none and ConnectMethod<,> carries no serializer, unlike
Grpc.Core.Method<,>. Recorded because the obvious 'fix' is to add them back.

The thing marshallers work around is absent. AGENTS.md is explicit that
GrpcProxyGenerator's marshaller pre-registration is load-bearing rather than an
optimisation, because MarshallerCache.CreateMarshaller<T> gates on CanSerialize,
which reaches DynamicStub -> MakeGenericType and returns false under AOT. Traced
the Connect path instead of assuming: codec.Read<T> -> TypeModel.Deserialize<T>
-> DeserializeRootImpl<T> -> GetSerializer<T> -> SerializerCache.Get<TProvider,T>,
a static generic field. DynamicStub appears only in the Type-based overloads,
none of which is on this path.

And a per-type marshaller could not work regardless: the server selects the codec
per request from the content-type, so a serializer baked into a method descriptor
cannot express content negotiation. Same fact as the ConnectCallInvoker being
binary-only, seen from the other side.

Nothing is lost. Caching a serializer per method would save a static field read.
ILC generates the instantiations without pre-registration because they are
statically reachable from generated code, which is why the native smoke test
round-trips rather than failing quietly. The one real consequence is that a
ConnectChannel is bound to a single TypeModel, the role BinderConfiguration
plays in protobuf-net.Grpc.

* Connect: resolve serializers once, not per message

Hoists the model lookup out of the per-request path. What it actually was,
read from the source: TryGetSerializer<T> is a static generic field read, a
virtual call on the model, and a second static field read - no dictionary and no
reflection, but per message, and 'the model is closed at compile time' ought to
mean the binding is made at compile time too.

Needs no change to protobuf-net.Core. SerializerCache.Get<TProvider,T>, both
State.Create overloads and DeserializeRoot/SerializeRoot are all public already;
the apparent blocker was that ProtoBufGeneratedServices is a private nested class
of the model and GetSerializer<T> is protected - but the model is partial, so
another part of the same class can name the nested type and hand the serializer
out. That accessor is hand-written in AotConnectSmoke for now and should become a
ProtoModelGenerator emit: it is useful to anything wanting to bind a serializer
once, not only to Connect.

The annotation trap is the part worth keeping. Annotating the codec's Read/Write
with ContractType - the obvious fix for the IL2091 that DeserializeRoot and
SerializeRoot raise - propagates the demand across the whole public generic
surface, reaching ConnectChannel and MeasuredCodecContent immediately and every
consumer's payload types eventually. That is the mistake AGENTS.md records
against ISerializer<T>, whose removal took AotSmoke from 200 warnings to 33.
Local UnconditionalSuppressMessage instead, as Core itself does in
GetSerializerAllowingReflection, justified exactly: both methods are
'serializer ?? TypeModel.GetSerializer<T>(Model)' and ?? does not evaluate its
right-hand side, so a supplied serializer makes the reflective arm unreachable.
Verified by reading both bodies.

Measured: 33 IL warnings before and after, +12 KB, 9/9 JIT and native. One

* notes/connect: can one type serve both Connect and gRPC?

Three layers. The attributes coexist and [ProtoService] is already shared, so
seeding needs no duplication; what collides is the emitted code - both
generators would emit a private parameterless constructor (CS0111), and
CreateClient<TService> only coexists by luck of differing parameter types, with
gRPC's an instance override from ClientFactory and ours static. Possible, but
needing the generators aware of each other. Two containers sharing the same
[ProtoService] lines is trivially safe; prefer that.

The sharp part is the server. gRPC and Connect use the identical URL path, so
mapping both puts two endpoints on one route. Probed by registering a second
MapPost at SayHello's path: startup SUCCEEDS, the duplicated path 500s with
AmbiguousMatchException at request time, and the three methods at distinct paths
are unaffected - a green startup with most of the service working and one method
broken.

The right shape is one handler dispatching on content-type, which is how
connect-go serves all three protocols on one port. ConnectContentType.TryParse
already separates codec from framing, and gRPC's framing is the same 5-byte
envelope layout Connect streaming uses, differing in the flag byte and in where
trailers go - so it is bounded work on machinery the streaming shapes need
anyway.

Also noted: Connect's path grammar allows a routing prefix, which would sidestep
the collision, and we do not support it - ConnectMethod hard-codes the path.

* Connect: server-streaming client, verified against connect-go

ConnectProbe reads 9/9 against demo.connectrpc.com, including a real

own server exists, so that a later disagreement has a known-good side.

Framing was probed first rather than read off the spec (notes §21): the
server-streaming *request* is enveloped too, so all three streaming shapes use
identical framing in both directions and differ only in cardinality. There is
one framing implementation to get right, which is also why duplex-first would
have bought no coverage that this does not.

Pieces: ConnectEnvelope (the 5-byte frame, layout-identical to gRPC's),
EndStreamReader for the terminator, EnvelopedCodecContent as the sibling
MeasuredCodecContent predicted, and ConnectServerStream<T> - an
IAsyncEnumerable<T> that additionally carries the metadata, since trailers now
arrive in the terminator rather than in headers and an IAsyncEnumerable has
nowhere to put them. Enumerable exactly once, and a stream that ends without a
terminator throws rather than reporting a short-but-clean result.

ConnectErrorReader gained TryParseObject so the error object has one parse and
two entry points: alone in a unary body, and nested under 'error' in a
terminator.

only via Microsoft.AspNetCore.App, which a client library has no business
requiring - so it is an explicit package reference, redundant from net10.0.

* Connect: server-streaming, end to end and verified both ways

Our client drives Eliza's server-streaming Introduce on demo.connectrpc.com, and
curl drives our server; our server's bytes are the shape connect-go produced -
enveloped messages, then a flags=0x02 terminator carrying metadata as name ->
[values]. AotConnectSmoke 13/13 JIT and native, ConnectProbe 9/9, native AOT
still 33 IL warnings and +173 KB.

This stage existed to falsify the §14.1 constraints rather than to add a feature,
so the verdict is the point. Four held unchanged. Most importantly the delegate-
per-shape rule: adding server-streaming was one new delegate type and one new
invoker, with zero changes to MapConnectService, to endpoint creation, or to the
error path. And trailers-behind-an-accessor would have hurt badly had it not
held, since streaming fills the same accessor from the terminating message rather
than from trailer- headers.

The fifth held in substance but was phrased wrongly, which is worth recording
because the wording would have misled whoever did this next. A streaming invoker
HAS to catch its own failures: once the first message is out the status is
committed to 200, so the endpoint's error path has nowhere to put them. What
actually holds is one exception TYPE and one decision about codes, reaching two
writers chosen by whether the response has started. ConnectException.HttpStatus
being null for the terminator case is load-bearing - it is how a caller tells a
service-reported error from an intermediary's 500 - and a check asserts it.

Two things §14.1 did not anticipate: content-type validation has to be
shape-aware, since the content-type states the framing and must agree with the
method's shape (415 either way, naming the framing to use); and Utf8JsonWriter
escapes '+' as \u002B, so 'application/connect+proto' never appears literally in
an error body - a check asserted the literal and failed.

* Connect: client-streaming, and the last §14.1 constraint properly tested

AotConnectSmoke 14/14 JIT and native; native AOT still 33 IL warnings.

Content-Length was the half-tested constraint. Server-streaming could not test it
properly - its response states no length but its request still can, being one
message - and client-streaming is the shape that cannot. Rather than assert it
from the client, which cannot see its own headers, the SERVICE reports what it
saw: CollectAsync returns HttpContext.Request.ContentLength ?? -1 and the check
requires -1, so 'the request went out chunked' is measured at the far end of a
real socket.

It cost almost nothing, which is the delegate-per-shape rule continuing to pay.
The response side is server-streaming's, reused verbatim: ClientStreamingAsync
builds a ConnectServerStream<TResponse> and takes the single message, so envelope
reading, the terminator, trailers and the error path are all shared. A count
other than one throws, since that is the peer disagreeing about the method. The
request side is one new HttpContent and one new invoker, and
EnvelopedRequestReader now serves both streaming invokers.

Two asymmetries recorded: a request stream has NO terminating message, since
end-of-stream is a response-only flag, so a partial envelope at the end is the
only detectable truncation; and a client-streaming body is not re-sendable, being
backed by an IAsyncEnumerable a caller may not be able to replay, so a retrying
handler fails rather than sending a partial body.

Also recorded because it is easy to get wrong: ReadAllAsync decodes each read's
messages into a list before advancing and yielding, because a ReadOnlySequence
cannot cross a yield AND the payloads reference the reader's buffer.

* Connect: duplex - all four method shapes now work

AotConnectSmoke 16/16, JIT and native. Native AOT is still 33 IL warnings; every
streaming shape added zero annotation debt.

Interleaving is proven rather than assumed. A duplex test that sends everything
then reads everything would pass over HTTP/1.1 against a server that drained
first, so the request producer waits for the echo of the previous message before
yielding the next: if HttpClient buffered the body, or the service drained before
replying, it deadlocks rather than failing. Three round-trips complete. That also
closes the open question about duplex HttpContent on SocketsHttpHandler.

Duplex added no protocol machinery, exactly as probing predicted. The client is
composition - the request body is client-streaming's EnvelopedStreamContent, the
response is server-streaming's ConnectServerStream - and the server invoker is
the server-streaming one with a sequence in place of a single request. Which
vindicates the build order: duplex-first would have exercised the same framing
while bundling two orthogonal risks.

Measured, and worth knowing: Kestrel will NOT serve h2c on a mixed plaintext
endpoint. HttpProtocols.Http1AndHttp2 without TLS answers a prior-knowledge
attempt with HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED rather than sniffing the connection preface, so a
plaintext deployment wanting duplex needs two listeners. The harness now has
both, and keeps the HTTP/1.1 claim honest: everything except duplex runs on the
HTTP/1.1 listener and the wire-form check still asserts it.

Both sides fail rather than deadlock. The server answers 505 if duplex arrives
over HTTP/1.1, and the client pins RequestVersionExact - because a plaintext
request left to negotiate settles on HTTP/1.1, where the client cannot read until
it has finished sending while the service waits for messages that never come.

* Connect: routing prefixes, and the latent Uri bug they exposed

The protocol allows a prefix in front of every method path, and §20 identified it
as the thing that lets Connect share a host with gRPC, since the two use
identical paths otherwise. Supported on both sides now; AotConnectSmoke maps the
same service at the root and under /rpc and drives both. 17/17, JIT and native,
still 33 IL warnings.

It exposed a bug that was already there. The channel resolved calls as
new Uri(baseAddress, method.Path), and Path has a leading slash - which makes it
an absolute-path reference, so Uri discards the base's own path entirely. Any
base address with a path was being silently ignored: a caller pointing at
http://host/api/ would have had calls go to http://host/. ConnectMethod now
carries RelativePath alongside Path and the channel combines with that.

Same trap one step earlier: a base address must end in '/' or Uri treats the last
segment as a file name and replaces it, so http://host/connect becomes
http://host/. The channel normalises rather than expecting callers to know.

Both produce a 404 against a correct server, which sends you looking in entirely
the wrong place.

method for contract-first, the serializer hoist becomes a case of it rather than
a separate hook, and a JSON codec becomes per-method too - which is how
contract-first would reach JsonFormatter/JsonParser. Three things want the same
refactor, which is usually the sign it is the right one.

implementing SerializationContext and DeserializationContext - the same machinery

Seed the model from [ProtoConnect], and add [NoSideEffects] for Connect GET (#1354)

Two gaps in the code-first Connect path, both found by writing a
consumer project **from the published
getting-started guide, step by step** — which nothing in either
repository had done before. Neither is
reachable from the existing harnesses, and the reason is worth keeping:
`AotConnectSmoke` lists
`[ProtoSerializable]` seeds explicitly, and `AotDualHostSmoke` declares
`[ProtoGrpc]` as well.

**Seeding.** `CollectPayloadsForModel` walked `[ProtoGrpc]` declarations
only, so a Connect-only project
got an *empty* `[ProtoModel]` — and an empty model emits nothing at all,
`Instance` included. The
consumer saw `CS0117` pointing into generated code, with no diagnostic
explaining it, on the first
example in the guide. The two container attributes are the same shape
and want the same payloads, so
the walk is now shared; `NamesModel` and `GetContracts` were already
attribute-agnostic.

**Connect GET.** The generator always left the descriptor's `idempotent`
flag at its `false` default, so
no code-first method was ever bound for `GET` and the client's `useGet`
had nothing to act on — a
feature the docs call the one thing Connect does that gRPC structurally
cannot. `[NoSideEffects]`
(shipping in protobuf-net.Connect, matched by full name) now supplies
it.

The name is the decision, and `[Idempotent]` was rejected: the proto
option has three levels and only
`NO_SIDE_EFFECTS` qualifies, because `IDEMPOTENT` means "safe to retry"
rather than "safe to cache and
prefetch". A delete is idempotent. `PBN5009` reports the attribute on a
non-unary operation **and** the
emitted descriptor ignores it there — reporting without ignoring would
bind a `GET` that cannot work.

Verified downstream against a real host: the GET is *observed* (a
middleware records the method each
